fri-sept-11---models-and-quantities.html
3 Fri Sept 11 - Models and quantities 3.1 Readings

3 Fri Sept 11 - Models and quantities Almost every biological theory or hypothesis is a model of how nature works. We use data to separate models that are more likely correct from ones that are less likely correct. Data are measured quantities and the model can be written clearly using mathematical and statistical notation and concepts. What kind of data do we need? Our model describes the signal and the noise Samples need to be representative of the population. This is best done by choosing them randomly. Assessing model fit and the ‘best’ model There can be multiple ways to correctly complete the statisics for your problem. And… there are some choices that are wrong. Types of measured quantities are: nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio. Which type of data you are using to test your biological hypotheses guides how you complete your statistical test. Measured quantities should have a name, symbol, a set of scaled numbers, units, and a procedural statement. Completing assignment 1 will help you understand what measured quantities are. This will help you understand the expectations for how should discuss your data in scientific writing and will prepare you for writing your statistical tests as equations, which allows you to communicate your biological hypotheses clearly. 3.1 Readings Ch1: Introduction by Quinn and Keough. Ch2.1: Definition of a measured quantity Ch2.2: Types of measurement and scale
mon-sept-14---equations-units-and-notation.html
4 Mon Sept 14 - Equations, units, and notation 4.1 Some common notations 4.2 Readings

4 Mon Sept 14 - Equations, units, and notation Units must balance across an equals. The hypothesis and assumptions for common statistical tests should be written as equations. Estimated coefficients and quantities, i.e., slopes, coefficients, and standard deviations have units. A data equation consists of model + residual. Statistical tests often assume the residual follows a probability distribution. Statistical models have explanatory variables and response variables. 4.1 Some common notations \(E(H)\) denotes the expected value. \(\hat{\beta}\) denotes an estimated value of \(\beta\). \(X\) denotes a realization of a random variable, where the random variable may follow a probability distribution such as \(P(X=x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}\). \(X \sim P(X=x)\) means ‘X is distributed as P(X=x)’. Note that it is not correct to say \(X\) is equal to \(P(X=x)\) is \(X\) is a realization from a probability distribution. 4.2 Readings Ch2.5: Ratio scale units Ch4: Equations Ch5: Data equations

37 Assignment 1 - Quantities (due Wed Sept 16)

37 Assignment 1 - Quantities (due Wed Sept 16) In the library or online, find a journal reporting research results, i.e., Ecology. Open the journal to an article, and list the first defined physical or biological quantity you encounter (if you must move to the next article, then so be it). For 4 different quantities, complete the following checklist: Journal name, volume, and page number: Name of quantity in words: symbol for quantity: number of values, n=: procedural statement (one sentence): Reproducible by another investigator ? type of measurement scale (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) If ratio scale: units = If a component is not present then state ‘not present.’

39 Assignment 3 - Hypothesis testing (due Fri Oct 2) Find, in the published literature, two mean values with associated standard deviations and sample size. Report the 6 values with full citation of source of the published data. Compute the t-statistic using the appropriate formula from Ch7.3. State which formula you used and why.
